assessment.summary: Documented AI harms are rising with adoption; the severe tail — misuse at scale or loss of control — is debated, but tracked and treated as a real risk by governments and intergovernmental bodies.
assessment.timeframe: Capabilities and adoption are advancing rapidly and documented incidents are rising; expert estimates of severe global outcomes span a very wide range.

claims.text: The total number of AI incidents and hazards reported in public media surged between 2022 and 2025, per OECD analysis of the OECD.AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM).

Media-reported AI incidents and hazards linked to synthetic media, child safety, and cyberattacks and fraud have more than doubled since 2022 (OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 53, February 2026).

NIST released the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) on 26 January 2023 to help manage risks to individuals, organizations, and society associated with artificial intelligence, and released a Generative AI Profile (NIST-AI-600-1) on 26 July 2024.

published.description: Risks from increasingly capable and widely deployed AI systems: documented present-day harms (synthetic media, fraud, cyberattacks, child-safety incidents), plus contested longer-term scenarios of large-scale misuse or loss of control. Governments and standards bodies now track incidents and publish risk-management frameworks, but quantified estimates of the severe tail remain scarce by nature.
published.name: Advanced AI Risk

assessment.summary: A present, quantified global decline in species and ecosystems — up to a million species threatened with extinction and most of the land and ocean already altered — with cascading risk to the food, water, and climate systems it underpins.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing decline over recent decades, with many losses (species extinctions, ecosystem tipping points) becoming irreversible within decades absent action.

claims.text: Up to 1 million species are threatened with extinction, many within decades, more than ever before in human history (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).
75 percent of the terrestrial environment has been severely altered to date by human actions, and 66 percent of the marine environment (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).
The current rate of global species extinction is tens to hundreds of times higher than the average over the last 10 million years, and it is accelerating (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).

published.description: An accelerating, human-driven decline in species and ecosystems that underpin food, water, and climate stability. Nature is being altered at a global scale and pace unprecedented in human history, with a growing share of the ecosystem services humanity depends on already in decline.
published.name: Biodiversity Loss and Ecosystem Collapse

assessment.summary: National cybersecurity commitments are improving but remain incomplete worldwide, and ransomware attacks on government services and breaches of core industries are already prominent documented threats — the tail risk is a cyberattack severe enough to disable critical infrastructure across multiple countries at once.
assessment.timeframe: Incident frequency and national preparedness are tracked annually; a severe multi-country outage could occur at any time given uneven critical-infrastructure protection.

claims.text: 139 countries have active Computer Incident Response Teams, with various levels of sophistication, up from 109 in the 2021 index, and 132 countries have a National Cybersecurity Strategy as of 2024, up from 107 in 2021 (ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024).

Worrisome threats highlighted in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024 include ransomware attacks targeting government services and other sectors, cyber breaches affecting core industries, costly system outages, and breaches of privacy for individuals and organizations.

NIST released version 2.0 of its Cybersecurity Framework on 26 February 2024; the framework was originally developed in 2014 to help protect critical infrastructure such as hospitals and power plants, and CSF 2.0 expands its scope to organizations in any sector.

published.description: A cyberattack severe enough to disable power grids, financial systems, water utilities, or other critical infrastructure across a wide area. National cybersecurity commitments are rising, but incident-response and critical-infrastructure-protection frameworks remain unevenly adopted worldwide, leaving gaps a sufficiently capable attacker could exploit.
published.name: Large-Scale Cyberattack on Critical Infrastructure

assessment.summary: Extreme (Carrington-class) storms are rare but historically documented; modern grid, satellite, and GPS dependence makes a repeat event far more disruptive than in 1859 or 1989, with credible multi-trillion-dollar damage estimates from U.S. federal sources.
assessment.timeframe: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center already issues routine G1-G4 storm watches and warnings; historical severe (G5-class) events cluster roughly once every few decades to a century, with no reliable short-term prediction of the next one.

claims.text: The 1859 Carrington Event, the largest geomagnetic storm in recorded history, crippled a large portion of the telegraph system across North America and Europe, with operators reporting fires from sparking equipment; on 13 March 1989, a severe geomagnetic storm took the Hydro-Québec electricity transmission system offline, leaving six million people without power for nine hours, many for days.

Citing the National Academies of Sciences, NOAA states that a Carrington-magnitude solar storm today has the potential to cost nearly $2 trillion, disrupting telecommunications, banking systems, GPS, and the energy grid, with an estimated 20-40 million people in the United States at risk of extended power outages lasting from 16 days to 1-2 years.

NOAA estimates the economic value of impacts to the U.S. electric power industry from a single geomagnetic storm event could range from $100 million for a small event up to $27 billion (2019 dollars) for a very large but unlikely event, and that a Carrington-level event could cause direct domestic economic damage of approximately $1.2 trillion over five months, with global impacts of $2.4 to $3.4 trillion over one year.

published.description: A severe solar eruption can drive strong electrical currents through Earth's surface, threatening power grids, satellites, GPS, radio, and aviation communications over a wide area. The 1859 Carrington Event, the largest geomagnetic storm on record, crippled telegraph systems across North America and Europe, and a March 1989 storm knocked out Hydro-Québec's grid, leaving six million people without power for nine hours. Modern societies are far more dependent on the electronics and satellite systems such storms disrupt: NOAA cites a National Academies of Sciences estimate that a Carrington-level storm today could put 20-40 million people in the United States at risk of extended power outages lasting from 16 days to 1-2 years, with total economic damage estimated at nearly $2 trillion.
published.name: Extreme Geomagnetic Storm (Solar Superstorm)

assessment.summary: A present, quantified toll of hundreds of thousands of conflict-related deaths a year across dozens of countries, with fatalities and the count of major wars both trending upward — carrying a real risk of wider regional escalation.
assessment.timeframe: Chronic and ongoing, with conflict-related fatalities at their highest annual level in years and the number of major conflicts rising.

claims.text: The number of locations of armed conflict fell slightly, from 51 states in 2023 to 49 in 2024, while the estimated overall number of fatalities rose from 188,000 in 2023 to 239,000 in 2024 — the highest annual total in the period 2018-24 (SIPRI Yearbook 2025).

There were five major armed conflicts involving over 10,000 estimated conflict-related fatalities in 2024, one more than in 2023: the Israel-Hamas and Russia-Ukraine wars, the civil wars in Myanmar and Sudan, and the subnational conflict in Ethiopia (SIPRI Yearbook 2025).
The number of high-intensity conflicts, with 1,000-9,999 estimated conflict-related fatalities, fell from 20 in 2023 to 19 in 2024 (SIPRI Yearbook 2025).

published.description: Ongoing state-based and civil wars that already kill hundreds of thousands annually and displace tens of millions more, with conflict-related fatalities and the number of major wars trending upward in recent years. Escalation, spillover between neighboring conflicts, and breakdown of humanitarian norms are the primary pathways to wider regional or global instability.
published.name: Global Armed Conflict

assessment.summary: A present, quantified global strain — hundreds of millions hungry, billions water-insecure — whose escalation pathways run through climate extremes and conflict.
assessment.timeframe: Chronic and ongoing; acute regional food crises recur annually, and climate change intensifies water stress through mid-century.

claims.text: An estimated 8.2 percent of the global population, about 673 million people, experienced hunger in 2024 (FAO, The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2025).
The global prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity was 28.0 percent in 2024, accounting for 2.3 billion people (FAO SOFI 2025).
266 million people are facing crisis levels of hunger or worse, according to the Global Report on Food Crises.
Roughly half of the world's population experiences severe water scarcity for at least part of the year (UN World Water Development Report 2024).
As of 2022, 2.2 billion people were without access to safely managed drinking water (UN World Water Development Report 2024).

published.description: A chronic global shortfall in access to adequate food and safe freshwater, driven by conflict, economic shocks, and climate extremes. Hundreds of millions face hunger and billions face water scarcity today; the tail risk is cascading food-system and water-supply failures that destabilize whole regions.
published.name: Global Food and Water Insecurity

assessment.summary: Over a hundred million people remain forcibly displaced worldwide — a standing stress on regional stability and the international protection system.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing at historic scale; direction depends on active conflicts, with returns in 2025 producing the first decline in ten years.

claims.text: At the end of 2025, 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced — roughly one in every 70 people (UNHCR Global Trends, June 2026).
Global refugee numbers fell by three per cent in 2025 to 41.6 million.
14.7 million displaced people went back to their areas or countries of origin in 2025, including 4.4 million refugees and 10.3 million internally displaced people.
70 per cent of refugees are living in protracted, long-term displacement situations (UNHCR Global Trends briefing, June 2026).

published.description: Displacement by persecution, conflict, violence, and human-rights violations at near-record scale. Sustained mass displacement strains host states and international institutions, and is both a symptom and an amplifier of instability; 2025 saw the first decline in a decade, driven by large-scale returns.
published.name: Global Forced Displacement Crisis

assessment.summary: An ongoing, human-caused warming of the climate system with civilizational-scale risks under continued high emissions.
assessment.timeframe: Already underway; impacts intensify with cumulative emissions.

claims.text: The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report attributes approximately 1.1 °C of global warming since 1850-1900 to human activities.

NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information ranked 2025 as the third-warmest year in the global temperature record dating back to 1850: the annual global surface temperature was 2.11°F (1.17°C) above the 20th-century average and 2.41°F (1.34°C) above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average, behind only 2024 and 2023. The ten warmest years in the 176-year record have all occurred since 2015, and upper-ocean heat content was record high in 2025.
NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory measured a monthly mean atmospheric CO2 concentration of 431.44 ppm at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii in June 2026, up from 429.61 ppm in June 2025.

published.description: Sustained warming of Earth's climate system driven by human greenhouse-gas emissions, with widespread impacts on weather extremes, sea level, ecosystems, and human systems. Unlike discrete events, it is an ongoing, intensifying process: 2025 was the third-warmest year on NOAA's global record (behind 2024 and 2023), the ten warmest years on record have all occurred since 2015, and atmospheric CO2 at NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory reached 431.44 ppm in June 2026, the highest level in over two million years.
published.name: Climate Change (Global Warming)

assessment.summary: A recurrent biological threat whose severe-pandemic form could greatly exceed the already-large annual burden of seasonal influenza.
assessment.timeframe: Pandemics recur on the order of every few decades; timing is not predictable.

claims.text: The WHO estimates that seasonal influenza causes about 290,000 to 650,000 respiratory deaths worldwide each year.
The WHO estimates that annual seasonal influenza epidemics result in about 3 to 5 million cases of severe illness worldwide.

published.description: A novel influenza strain to which the population has little immunity could spread worldwide and cause mortality far exceeding ordinary seasonal influenza, as in 1918. Influenza pandemics have recurred several times per century.
published.name: Influenza Pandemic

assessment.summary: A rare, high-consequence impact; no known large object currently threatens Earth, though the catalogue of hazardous-size objects is incomplete.
assessment.timeframe: No known object of concern is on an impact trajectory this century.

claims.text: NASA reports that no known asteroid larger than 140 meters has a significant chance of hitting Earth for the next 100 years.
NASA reports that fewer than half of the estimated 25,000 near-Earth objects 140 meters and larger have been found to date.
With over 90% of the near-Earth objects larger than one kilometer already discovered, NASA's NEO Observations Program is now focusing on finding 90% of the NEO population larger than 140 meters.

Asteroid 2024 YR4 reached a peak Earth-impact probability of 4.3% in February 2025, the highest ever recorded for an asteroid of its size, before NASA concluded (using James Webb Space Telescope data from February 2026) that the object poses no significant impact risk to Earth in 2032 and beyond, and ruled out any chance of it impacting the Moon on 22 December 2032.

published.description: A sufficiently large near-Earth object striking Earth would cause regional to continental devastation. NASA's Planetary Defense effort catalogues and tracks the larger near-Earth object population to assess impact hazards decades in advance. The system was tested in 2024-2026 by asteroid 2024 YR4, which briefly reached the highest Earth-impact probability ever recorded for an object of its size before follow-up observations, including from the James Webb Space Telescope, ruled out any impact risk.
published.name: Near-Earth Asteroid Impact

assessment.summary: Thousands of warheads remain in military stockpiles — thousands deployed, and roughly two thousand on high alert — making nuclear war a persistent, low-probability, civilization-scale risk.
assessment.timeframe: No reliable forecast; risk tracks geopolitical crises, arsenal modernization, and the erosion or renewal of arms-control agreements.

claims.text: SIPRI estimates a total global inventory of 12,187 nuclear warheads in January 2026, of which about 9,745 were in military stockpiles for potential use.

An estimated 4,012 warheads were deployed with missiles and aircraft in January 2026, and between 2,100 and 2,200 of the deployed warheads were kept in a state of high operational alert on ballistic missiles.
Nine states possess nuclear weapons: the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, China, India, Pakistan, North Korea and Israel.

published.description: A deliberate or inadvertent nuclear exchange between states. Global arsenals remain in the thousands of warheads, all nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their forces, and hundreds of weapons are kept on high operational alert — keeping a civilization-scale exchange a persistent possibility even at low annual probability.
published.name: Nuclear War

assessment.summary: A continent-scale disaster with extremely low annual probability and no current signs of imminent eruption.
assessment.timeframe: No reliable short-term forecast. The three largest past eruptions occurred ~2.1M, ~1.3M, and ~0.64M years ago.

claims.text: The USGS estimates the annual probability of a Yellowstone supereruption at roughly 1 in 730,000.
Yellowstone has produced three caldera-forming eruptions in the past ~2.1 million years.

published.description: A large caldera system beneath Yellowstone National Park capable of a 'supereruption' that would blanket much of North America in ash and inject climate-altering aerosols into the stratosphere. Such eruptions are extraordinarily rare and there is no evidence one is imminent.
published.name: Yellowstone Supervolcano
